title: Can we have a film or short film with no plot, no characters, and no theme?

commenti.body: There have been several experimental films exclusively focused on extended, unassuming views—either a prolonged zoom out of a window or a static shot capturing a skyscraper. Ironically, all these films have attained feature length. I guess making a short film of this idea shouldn't be that challenging.

You might be interested in the silent films of the Dadaist movement. Rene Clair’s Entre’act comes to mind. I’m oversimplifying a bit because it was a response to the horror of WW1, but part of the point was to create entertaining “nonsense”
there are many short films that are just abstract images [going back to the silent era](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SDxcfDNFrIA)
Perfect exemple. Walter Ruttmann is mostly known for Berlin: Symphony of a Metropolis, which is again, Feature lengths. Also I think the OP should check out Le Chien Andalou, if he hasn't already.

> Le Chien Andalou

except that has a plot, character, and theme

Honestly, man, I think theme kind of inherently emerges from any film, no matter how abstract. Some one else mentioned Dada absurdity as a response to World War I, but isn't fracturing meaning to highly the illogic of existence a theme? Even hyper-minimal "Is it even film?" stuff like Anthony McCall's Light Describing A Cone or Nam June Paik's Zen For Film could be ascribed a number of conceptual themes. 

Basically, even if you omit every other aspect of filmmaking, the very act of taking a specific thing and making someone else look at it creates some kind of theme, even if that specific thing is nothing.

I'm not entirely certain it has a defined plot. Primarily, it appears to be a compilation of surreal imagery. While it certainly features characters and possibly conveys a theme, there is still uncertainty about the exact theme of the film.

Maybe, I mean the closest I've seen to a themeless film is Fantasia. The whole thing is just a bunch of animated sequences with music played over them, and while some sequences have themes in them, others like the dancing animals sequence(I think, I haven't watched it in a while), and the Rite Of Spring sequence doesn't seem to have one, with the dancing animals sequence just being a bunch of anthropomorphic animals with some attire dancing, and the Rite Of Spring sequence just being an illustrated chronologically of the earth's history. Plus, the whole thing itself doesn't seem to be doing all of this for a thematic reason, but seemingly just because.

There are abstract film pieces e.g. by Stan Brakhage and Lee Hangjun. You might want to check this list on RYM, I've found many such pieces on that. https://rateyourmusic.com/film_genre/Abstract%20Film/
I can describe what happens in the film, which is a plot to a certain extent. I couldn't describe the plot of Koyaanisqatsi.
